words.etymon: unmapped in slab (word absent from the slab's word list; context-before line CatAgr 132.2 w1/2); analysis *dyew- + *ph₂tḗr

cognate: Ved. dyaúṣ pitā́ (nom.; voc. dyaùṣ pítar) = Lat. Iū-piter / Diēs-piter = Gk Ζεῦ πάτερ, all *dyéw- + *ph₂tḗr 'Sky (god)' + 'father'; both members cognate in all three branches
drift_or_renewal: Latin univerbated the (vocative) phrase *dyeu ph₂ter into a proper name Iupiter/Diespiter, with 'father' no longer transparent; the oblique cases use the bare stem (Ioui). Vedic keeps a free two-word phrase (nominative in the AV anchors, vocative in RV 6.51.5), Greek keeps it as a vocative address (support only: no slab Greek passage has it)
shared_syntax: theonym *dyēws with appositive *ph₂tḗr as its fixed epithet (epithet + noun), used in naming/address of the sky-god; in Vedic regularly paired with Earth as mother (pṛthivī mātā)
context: Both anchors name the sky-god as father in a ritual or hymnic setting: AVŚ 3.23.6, a fertility charm calling on plants 'whose father is Dyaus, mother Earth'; AVŚ 9.10.12 (= RV 1.164.33), a cosmogonic hymn 'Dyaus is our father, begetter'; Cato Agr. 132, the dapes prayer to Iupiter Dapalis (offering of daps and wine) in a farm-ritual text. Why not chance: 'pater' is a productive Latin epithet of gods (Mars pater, Cato 141), so the case does not rest on 'a god called father'. It rests on the exact match of both members, the sky-god noun *dyēws and *ph₂tḗr, across Indic, Greek and Latin, with Latin fusing the pair into one word, which only an old fixed phrase explains. Cato passage is research_only in the slab.

note: One claim (Dyēus ph₂tēr). Considered and not filed: language-of-gods-vs-men (Cratylus 392a; no non-Greek slab passage), land/earth as mother (Isocr./Lysias autochthony ~ AVŚ 12.1.12: universal motif, earth word renewed), upper/lower polar pair adhara/uttara ~ Av. aδara/upara ~ Lat. inferus/superus (generic, contexts not congruent), OE heard hond-locen ~ κρατεραῖσι λύγοισι (contexts not congruent), wake-from-sleep h₁ger-/swep- (generic), daps ~ δαπανᾶν in sacrifice (word, not phrase).
